title: Does the Indus script encode language, or a non-linguistic sign system?
short: Whether the short Harappan inscriptions record speech at all has been argued with entropy statistics for two decades; no test yet separates writing from emblem systems decisively.
matters: If the Indus signs are writing, the Harappan civilization was literate and every proposed decipherment (Dravidian, Indo-Aryan, Munda or other) is a legitimate project; if not, it becomes the main case of a large urban society administered without writing, which changes comparative accounts of states and bureaucracy. The answer also governs how seals, tags and pot inscriptions are read as evidence for trade, taxation and identity across a region of perhaps a million square kilometres.
stuck: Inscriptions average about five signs and the longest have only a few dozen, so statistical signatures that distinguish languages from other systems are weak at this length. Farmer, Sproat and Witzel (2004) argued the brevity and sign-repetition patterns are incompatible with writing; Rao et al. (2009) answered that conditional entropy places the corpus within the range of linguistic scripts; Sproat (2010, 2014) showed that several non-linguistic systems also fall in that range. The corpora used by different teams differ in sign lists (roughly 400 to 700 signs) and inclusion rules, and the most complete database (ICIT) requires permission to access.
solved: A pre-registered battery of measures, fixed before the Indus data are scored, classifies a large set of known writing systems and non-linguistic systems (heraldry, mason's marks, deity symbols, administrative codes) correctly when all are trimmed to the Indus length distribution, and then assigns the Indus corpus to one class with stated error rates that are robust to choice of sign list.
approach: The corpus rests on decades of human labour: the concordance of Mahadevan (1977), the photographic volumes of the CISI edited by Joshi (1987), Shah (1991) and Parpola (2010), and the ICIT database described by Wells (2015) and Fuls (2023). The statistical debate runs from Farmer (2004) through Rao (2009), Yadav (2010), Lee (2010) and Sproat (2010) to Sproat (2014) and Nair (2026).

Reconcile the Mahadevan, CISI and ICIT sign lists into an open, versioned corpus with a concordance between numbering systems. How variant signs are merged or split is the decision that shapes every later statistic, so alternatives should be kept side by side rather than settled silently.

Build comparison corpora of known scripts and non-linguistic systems, sampled to match Indus text lengths, object types and sign inventories, extending the dataset of Sproat (2014). Short texts are the core difficulty, since many measures that separate language from emblem systems lose power on inscriptions of five signs or fewer.

The linguistic and non-linguistic hypotheses should be tested on what they predict differently, such as sign-position regularities, reuse of sequences across object types and sites, and behaviour on longer texts, rather than on entropy alone.

Fix the classifiers and thresholds in a public pre-registration, then report results across alternative segmentations and sign lists. The outcome will likely be a graded likelihood rather than a verdict, and epigraphers and linguists should review it before it is cited.

Progress depends on negotiated open access to ICIT and to the CISI photographic archive, and on recording unpublished excavated material held by the Archaeological Survey of India and the Department of Archaeology and Museums, Pakistan.

existing.title: The Indus Script: Texts, Concordance and Tables
existing.venue: Memoirs of the Archaeological Survey of India 77. New Delhi: Archaeological Survey of India
existing.note: Computer-generated concordance of the texts then known, with sign frequencies, positions and site distributions; still the most widely used reference sign list.

existing.authors: Jagat Pati Joshi and Asko Parpola (eds.)
existing.title: Corpus of Indus Seals and Inscriptions, vol. 1: Collections in India
existing.venue: Annales Academiae Scientiarum Fennicae / Memoirs of the Archaeological Survey of India 86. Helsinki: Suomalainen Tiedeakatemia
existing.note: First volume of the photographic corpus (CISI); later volumes cover Pakistan (1991) and new material and collections elsewhere (2010 onward).

existing.authors: Sayid Ghulam Mustafa Shah and Asko Parpola (eds.)
existing.title: Corpus of Indus Seals and Inscriptions, 2: Collections in Pakistan
existing.venue: Helsinki: Suomalainen Tiedeakatemia (Annales Academiae Scientiarum Fennicae B 240)
existing.note: Photographic corpus of Indus inscribed objects in Pakistani collections, including Mohenjo-daro and Harappa finds.

existing.title: Deciphering the Indus Script
existing.note: Synthesis arguing that the script is logo-syllabic writing of a Dravidian language, with rebus-based readings of selected signs.

existing.authors: Steve Farmer, Richard Sproat and Michael Witzel
existing.title: The Collapse of the Indus-Script Thesis: The Myth of a Literate Harappan Civilization
existing.note: Argued from text brevity, sign repetition and the rarity of singleton signs that the Indus signs are non-linguistic symbols.

existing.authors: Rajesh P. N. Rao, Nisha Yadav, Mayank N. Vahia, Hrishikesh Joglekar, R. Adhikari and Iravatham Mahadevan
existing.title: Entropic Evidence for Linguistic Structure in the Indus Script
existing.note: Showed that the conditional entropy of Indus sign sequences falls between rigid and random systems, in the range of known languages.

existing.authors: Rob Lee, Philip Jonathan and Pauline Ziman
existing.title: Pictish Symbols Revealed as a Written Language through Application of Shannon Entropy
existing.venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society A 466 (2121): 2545–2560
existing.note: Applied a related entropy method to Pictish stones; frequently cited in the Indus debate as an example of how such measures can classify non-linguistic systems as writing.

existing.authors: Nisha Yadav, Hrishikesh Joglekar, Rajesh P. N. Rao, Mayank N. Vahia, Ronojoy Adhikari and Iravatham Mahadevan
existing.title: Statistical Analysis of the Indus Script Using n-Grams
existing.note: n-gram models found strong directional and positional structure consistent with a formal language, while stating that this does not by itself prove the encoding of speech.

existing.title: Ancient Symbols, Computational Linguistics, and the Reviewing Practices of the General Science Journals
existing.note: Criticized the entropy argument and showed that non-linguistic systems can produce similar values; Rao et al. replied in the following issue.

existing.authors: Asko Parpola, B. M. Pande and Petteri Koskikallio (eds.)
existing.title: Corpus of Indus Seals and Inscriptions, 3.1: New Material, Untraced Objects and Collections outside India and Pakistan, Mohenjo-daro and Harappa
existing.venue: Helsinki: Suomalainen Tiedeakatemia (Annales Academiae Scientiarum Fennicae Humaniora 359)
existing.note: Adds new and previously untraced inscribed material from Mohenjo-daro and Harappa to the corpus.

existing.title: A Statistical Comparison of Written Language and Nonlinguistic Symbol Systems
existing.note: Compiled corpora of non-linguistic systems and found that no single published measure cleanly separates them from writing; the closest existing template for a controlled test.

existing.authors: Bryan K. Wells and Andreas Fuls
existing.title: The Archaeology and Epigraphy of Indus Writing
existing.note: Presents the ICIT database with Fuls's appendices on automated segmentation, positional analysis and classification of undeciphered writing systems.

existing.title: A Catalog of Indus Signs
existing.note: Sign-by-sign frequencies and positional behaviour keyed to his Corpus of Indus Inscriptions (2022, over 5,500 texts), concluding the script is logo-syllabic with about 700 signs.

existing.title: Semantic scope of Indus inscriptions comprising taxation, trade and craft licensing, commodity control and access control: archaeological and script-internal evidence
existing.note: Argues from object context and sign structure that inscriptions served administrative functions, a reading compatible with logographic writing.

existing.title: How Non-Linguistic Is the Indus Sign System? A Synthetic-Baseline Scorecard
existing.note: Scores 1,916 deduplicated inscriptions against simulated heraldic and administrative baselines and seven real non-linguistic corpora, finding that none reproduces the Indus profile; not yet peer reviewed.

archives.repository: Finnish Academy of Science and Letters, Helsinki, with the Archaeological Survey of India and Department of Archaeology and Museums, Pakistan
archives.collection: Corpus of Indus Seals and Inscriptions (CISI), vols. 1 (1987), 2 (1991), 3.1 (2010) and later parts
archives.note: Photographic corpus of seals and inscribed objects arranged by collection (Joshi and Parpola (1987), Shah and Parpola (1991), Parpola et al. (2010)); published in print, with the underlying photographs not openly available online.

holdings.name: CISI vol. 1: Collections in India (Joshi and Parpola, 1987)
holdings.note: Photographic corpus of seals and inscribed objects in Indian collections; the URL is a bibliographic record.

holdings.name: CISI vol. 2: Collections in Pakistan (Shah and Parpola, 1991)
holdings.note: Photographic corpus of inscribed objects in Pakistani collections, including Mohenjo-daro and Harappa finds; the URL is a bibliographic record.

holdings.name: CISI vol. 3, part 1: Mohenjo-daro and Harappa (Parpola, Pande and Koskikallio, 2010)
holdings.note: New and previously untraced material from the two largest sites.

archives.repository: Interactive Corpus of Indus Texts (ICIT), Technische Universität Berlin
archives.collection: Relational database of inscribed objects, texts and sign list compiled by Bryan K. Wells and Andreas Fuls
archives.note: Over 4,500 inscribed objects and 5,500 texts with analysis tools; access is by request to the administrator.

archives.repository: Harappa.com (Jonathan Mark Kenoyer, Richard H. Meadow and colleagues)
archives.collection: Images and reports from the Harappa Archaeological Research Project, including excavated seals, tablets and inscribed pottery
archives.note: Open image collection with stratigraphic context for many Harappa inscriptions, useful for dating and object-type controls.

archives.collection: Harappan Gallery: seals and sealings from Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Lothal and other sites allocated to India
archives.note: Major holding of Indus seals; images available through CISI vol. 1 and partly online, with study access by application.

archives.repository: Archaeological Survey of India / Department of Archaeology and Museums, Pakistan
archives.collection: Excavated material from Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Dholavira, Kalibangan, Rakhigarhi and other sites, including unpublished inscribed objects
archives.note: Recent excavations have added inscriptions not yet in the corpora; recording them requires collaboration with the excavating authorities.
